questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Standing and select committees
questions.learningObjective: classify a committee by its duration and brief
questions.stem: A legislature creates three committees: one that lives for the life of the chamber and reviews bills, one appointed to examine a single named subject and then report on it, and one drawn from both chambers to consider a matter of common concern. How is the first of the three classified?

options.text: A joint committee, because a joint body is the one that keeps a permanent brief
options.misconception: reverses the feature that makes a body joint, which is membership of both chambers

options.text: A select committee, because it examines one subject and reports on that subject once
options.misconception: calls a continuing body a body appointed for a single subject

options.text: A sub-committee, because a body that reports to a chamber is delegated by it
options.misconception: treats appointment by a chamber as delegation from a committee

options.text: A standing committee, because it continues for the chamber's life and keeps a standing brief

questions.explanation: Committees are classified by two features: how long they last and what they are for. A standing committee has a continuing brief and exists for the life of the chamber, which is what the first body is described as. A select committee is appointed to look into one question and dissolves once it reports, which describes the second. A joint committee draws its members from both chambers, which describes the third, and that feature has nothing to do with duration. A sub-committee is appointed by another committee rather than by the chamber, so the fourth option names a different relationship again.
questions.hint: Ask whether the body outlives the matter it was set up to examine.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The committee of the whole
questions.learningObjective: identify what changes when a chamber sits as a committee
questions.stem: A bill is reached in a chamber and the Speaker announces that the chamber will resolve itself into a committee of the whole so the measure can be considered clause by clause without moving between sittings. What follows from that announcement?

options.text: The members lose their votes until the chamber resumes its ordinary form
options.misconception: assumes sitting in committee suspends members' voting rights

options.text: The Speaker vacates the chair, so amendments may be moved to any clause of the measure
The quorum rule stops applying for the duration of the sitting
options.misconception: reads a change of form as an end to the requirement of a quorum

options.text: A recorded division becomes the only available way to dispose of a clause
options.misconception: makes a division compulsory where the sitting itself is the mechanism

questions.explanation: A committee of the whole is the same set of members sitting in a different form so that the Speaker can leave the chair, usually for another member to take it, and detailed amendments can be moved while remaining members take part. Nothing is taken away from the members: they debate, they move amendments, and the whole chamber still votes on the measure when the committee reports. The quorum rule continues to apply, because the members present are the same members as before. And nothing about the sitting makes a division necessary, since disposing of the measure is done by the chamber at the end, not by counting votes clause by clause.
questions.hint: Ask which of the members' ordinary powers the announcement takes away.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Quorum for a division
questions.learningObjective: compute a quorum and a majority of those present
questions.stem: A chamber of 90 members fixes its quorum at one third of the whole chamber and decides ordinary questions by a simple majority of those present and voting. On a sitting at which exactly the quorum is present, how many must vote in favour for a question to carry?

options.text: 15, because a question carries when the votes are evenly divided
options.misconception: treats a tie as a carried question, which it is not

options.text: 23, because a majority of the whole chamber is always required
options.misconception: replaces a majority of those voting with a majority of the chamber

options.text: 16, because a quorum is always the next whole number above a third
options.misconception: rounds an exact third up instead of recognising it as a whole number

options.text: 16, because one third of 90 is 30 and half of 30 is 15

questions.explanation: The quorum is one third of 90, which is exactly 30 and needs no rounding, so a sitting of exactly 30 is quorate. The question then needs a simple majority of those present and voting, and a simple majority of 30 is 16, since 15 votes to 15 is a tie and a tie is not carried. The 23 in the second option comes from treating the rule as a majority of the whole chamber, which is 46 and a different rule entirely. The third option invents a rounding step for a figure that is already whole. Both routes to 16 agree, which is the check that the answer is right.
questions.hint: Work out the quorum first, then take a simple majority of that number.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What a recorded division shows
questions.learningObjective: read a division list and state what it establishes

stimulus.body: Extract from a division list, written for this question. Question put: that the amendment be agreed to. Members present at the division: 90. AYES: 44. NOES: 38. Abstentions: 0. Members not voting: 8. The standing orders of the chamber require a quorum of one third of the whole chamber and decide questions by a simple majority of those present and voting. The published list records the number voting on each side of a question. It does not record the names of individual members, and no account of the speeches taken in the debate is attached to it.

questions.stem: A division list records a vote on an amendment: 90 members present, 44 AYES, 38 NOES and no abstentions, so 8 members did not vote, and the standing orders quoted alongside it set a quorum of one third and a simple majority of those voting. What does the list establish, and what does it leave out?

options.text: It establishes only the numbers on each side, not even whether the amendment carried
options.misconception: denies a result the numbers and the rule in the extract make plain

options.text: It establishes each member's party and how that party voted as a single bloc
options.misconception: reads party positions out of a list the extract says names no individuals

options.text: It establishes the numbers on each side and that the amendment carried, not what was said
It establishes that the amendment carried and the arguments made on both sides
options.misconception: credits the list with a record of the debate the extract says is not attached

questions.explanation: The arithmetic settles the result. A quorum of one third of 90 is 30, and 90 members were present, so the sitting was quorate. Those present and voting number 44 plus 38, which is 82, and a simple majority of 82 is 42, so 44 AYES against 38 NOES carried the amendment by six votes. What the list does not carry is any account of the case: the extract says expressly that no speech is attached and that no individual member is named, so a reader cannot learn from it why members voted as they did or which party pressed which argument. The third option is simply wrong about the arithmetic, and the fourth asks the list to do what the extract says it cannot.
questions.hint: Check the quorum and the majority first, then ask what the extract says the list leaves out.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reading a roll-call record for discipline
questions.learningObjective: test a comparative claim against its denominator
questions.stem: A party in a chamber publishes a table showing that 94 percent of its members voted with the party line in every division the chamber recorded, and a researcher concludes from it that the party is the most disciplined in that chamber. Recorded divisions are only a minority of the votes taken. What follows?

options.text: The table cannot be used at all, because the unrecorded votes are the greater part
options.misconception: dismisses a figure that remains valid for the subset it actually covers

options.text: The table supports a claim about the recorded divisions, not about the chamber as a whole
The table disproves discipline, since a six percent deviation is a serious breach
options.misconception: turns a high rate of agreement into evidence against discipline

options.text: The table supports the comparative claim, because the unrecorded votes are a fair sample
options.misconception: treats the recorded divisions as an unbiased sample of all votes taken

questions.explanation: A rate is only ever a rate of something, and the something here is the recorded divisions. 94 percent is a share of the party's votes in that subset, so it is a genuine and substantial measure of agreement in those divisions and nothing more. It does not extend to the divisions nobody recorded, and the extract says the parties' figures in the other parties' divisions are not in the table either, so the word most in the researcher's claim has no basis at all. The unrecorded votes are not a fair sample precisely because contested measures are the ones that tend to be recorded. Neither over-reading nor dismissing the figure is right: it is usable, within its own scope.
questions.hint: Ask what population the percentage is a percentage of.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The party unit and the whip
questions.learningObjective: name the arrangement that produces party voting in a chamber
questions.stem: In a chamber that operates on party lines, members of the same party are expected to vote together on the strength of instructions carried by an official the party appoints for that purpose. What is this arrangement, and what does it deliver?

options.text: Party discipline, which delivers reliable party voting inside the chamber
Party registration, which delivers a public list of every member's party
options.misconception: confuses the label attached to a member with the voting behaviour of a group

options.text: The collective responsibility convention, which binds a cabinet to speak with one voice
options.misconception: imports a rule that binds an executive into a description of a caucus

options.text: The casting rule, which gives a deciding vote to a party's longest-serving member
options.misconception: mistakes a single deciding vote for an instruction-carrying organisation

questions.explanation: The arrangement described is the party whip, and the behaviour it produces is party discipline: members voting with the line their party has settled. The officer transmits instructions so that members are not each left to calculate the party interest for themselves on every question. The other three names do not fit. Party registration is only the fact of being entered on a party's roll, and says nothing about how a member votes. The casting rule concerns a single deciding vote when numbers are level, and involves no instructions at all. Collective responsibility binds the members of a government to support each other, which is a rule about a cabinet rather than about a caucus in a chamber.
questions.hint: Ask what the appointed official actually carries, and who is bound by it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Seat concentration and the law of 1/n
questions.learningObjective: explain why a large party gains more easily from surplus votes
questions.stem: A chamber of 90 seats is held by three blocs of 46, 30 and 14, and the largest bloc governs alone. The law of the one over n says the larger a party, the more of the surplus votes below the majority threshold it can expect to pick up. Why is that advantage there?

options.text: A large party needs a smaller slice of the surplus to gain its next seat
A large party's surplus is smaller, so each surplus vote counts for more
options.misconception: assumes the surplus shrinks as the party grows, which it does not

options.text: A large party wins districts outright, so it needs no surplus at all
options.misconception: invents a district system and removes the surplus from the calculation

options.text: A large party needs more surplus votes but wins them more often
options.misconception: contradicts itself, since needing more votes cannot be an advantage

questions.explanation: The advantage is arithmetic, and this chamber shows it. The majority of 90 is 46, so the surplus is 44 votes, and those surplus votes are what decide the seats above the minimum. Under the divisor method a bloc on n seats needs a share of the surplus equal to 1 divided by the number of the seat it is contesting. The bloc of 46 is contesting its 47th seat and so needs 44 divided by 47, which is 0.94 of a vote and therefore one whole surplus vote. The bloc of 14 is contesting its 15th and needs 44 divided by 15, which is 2.93 and therefore three. The bigger party is the one closer to a cheap next seat, which is the whole content of the law.
questions.hint: Compare what each bloc would have to win out of the surplus for one more seat.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Pairs that reach two-thirds of a chamber
questions.learningObjective: count which partnerships clear a supermajority threshold
questions.stem: Three blocs of 46, 30 and 14 seats fill a chamber of 90, and a measure needs the votes of two-thirds of the whole chamber, that is 60. How many of the three possible two-bloc partnerships reach 60, and which single partnership lands on the threshold exactly?

options.text: Two of them, and the partnership of 46 with 14 reaches 60 exactly
Three of them, and the partnership of 30 with 14 reaches 60 exactly
options.misconception: counts a partnership that falls sixteen short and gives it the exact total

options.text: Two of them, and the partnership of 46 with 30 reaches 60 exactly
options.misconception: names the partnership that clears the threshold by sixteen votes as if it landed on it

options.text: One of them, and the partnership of 46 with 14 reaches 60 exactly
options.misconception: excludes a partnership that meets the threshold as well as one that exceeds it

questions.explanation: Two-thirds of 90 is 60, and the three partnerships must be added out: 46 plus 30 is 76 and clears the threshold by sixteen; 46 plus 14 is exactly 60 and clears it; 30 plus 14 is 44 and falls sixteen short. So two of the three reach 60, and only the 46 and 14 partnership lands on the number exactly. The second option names the partnership that overshoots as though it were exact, the third drops a partnership that does reach the threshold, and the fourth counts a sum of 44 as though it were 60. Each is a different slip about the same three additions, which is why checking them is enough to settle the item.
questions.hint: Write out all three pair sums and compare each with 60.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The Speaker's procedural role
questions.learningObjective: describe the presiding officer's function
questions.stem: A chamber's presiding officer applies the standing orders, rules on points of order, decides whether a proposed amendment is in order, keeps order in the chamber, and votes only where the standing orders allow. Which description fits that set of powers?

options.text: To choose which measures are taken up in the chamber's business
options.misconception: turns an adjudicating function into a control over the order of business

options.text: To represent the chamber in its dealings with the other chamber
options.misconception: assigns an inter-chamber function the listed powers do not contain

options.text: To hold a deciding vote whenever the parties are evenly divided
options.misconception: makes a casting vote general when the stem limits voting in one direction only

options.text: To preside over the chamber's proceedings under its standing orders

questions.explanation: Every one of the powers listed is an exercise of presiding: applying the rules, ruling on points of order, judging the admissibility of amendments and keeping order. That is what presiding over proceedings under the standing orders means, and the rule that the officer does not vote is part of the same idea, because the chair is a referee rather than a participant. The other descriptions each attach a function the list does not contain. Dealing with the other chamber is a separate representational role, choosing the order of business is a power some presiding officers have but is not what the list describes, and a deciding vote is exercised only where the rules allow it, which the stem says is an exception rather than the rule.
questions.hint: Check whether each power listed is about the conduct of proceedings.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The second reading as the policy debate
questions.learningObjective: explain the function of a restricted-amendment stage
questions.stem: Under a three-reading procedure a measure is read once and its general principle is debated at the second reading, where amendments to the principle are allowed but amendments to the detail are not. What does that restriction buy?

options.text: It sends the detail of the measure to a select committee and nowhere else
options.misconception: treats a procedural restriction as a rule about where business is transacted

options.text: It lets the principle be voted on without any debate whatever
options.misconception: claims the opposite of what a debate stage is for

options.text: It concentrates argument on the principle before the detail is opened up
It stops members amending the measure at any later stage at all
options.misconception: extends the restriction to stages where detailed amendments are normal

questions.explanation: The restriction is a way of sequencing the argument. If amendments to the detail were allowed at the second reading, a chamber would spend its time on words in a clause before it had decided whether the measure ought to exist at all, and the decision about the principle would be reached piecemeal. Holding the detail back means the question of whether the policy is wanted is settled first, and the clause-by-clause work follows with a settled principle behind it. Detailed amendments remain open at the later stages, so the second option overstates the restriction, and the third and fourth both claim effects the restriction does not produce: business is not diverted by a rule about amendment, and the second reading is where the debate on principle takes place.
questions.hint: Ask what the chamber would have to decide before the detail can be argued.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A consent bill and the executive's timetable
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose of a procedure that saves sitting time
questions.stem: A government introduces a measure that a member has already announced his party will oppose, and the chamber's rules allow the measure to be taken at the end of the day's business without counting it out at the time set for votes. What is the point of that allowance?

options.text: It lets the government put the measure through without ever debating it
options.misconception: claims a saving of time removes the requirement to debate

options.text: It removes the need for a majority, so the measure takes effect as agreed
options.misconception: converts a time-saving device into a change in the voting rule

options.text: It obliges the opposition to put its objections in writing beforehand
options.misconception: invents a documentary precondition the procedure does not mention

options.text: It saves sitting time by not setting aside a slot for the count on each measure

questions.explanation: A fixed order of business normally reserves a stretch of the day's sitting for counting the votes on measures, and every measure that does not need a count occupies time that then goes unused. Letting a government whose measure is certain to be opposed take it at the end of the day removes it from that list, and the time saved can be used on measures that do need debate. The device is a scheduling arrangement. It says nothing about how many votes are required, so a measure still needs a majority, and it says nothing about debate, which the government may still have to concede. Nor does it require the opposition to file anything, since the announcement of opposition was the very fact that made the allowance usable.
questions.hint: Ask what the saving of time is being spent on.

questions.topic: A private member's bill
questions.learningObjective: identify a member's own measure and its standing
questions.stem: A member who holds no ministerial office introduces a measure confined to the arrangements of his own district, and no minister will sponsor it. What is such a measure called, and what is its standing in the chamber?

options.text: A private member's bill, a measure the government has already agreed to support
options.misconception: describes government backing, which the stem expressly rules out

options.text: A delegated instrument, made under a power already given to an official
options.misconception: confuses a member's own proposal with an act of a delegated authority

options.text: A consent measure, which takes effect without any vote being taken at all
options.misconception: invents an automatic effect that no chamber grants to members' measures

options.text: A private member's bill, a measure with no sponsor anywhere in the government

questions.explanation: A measure introduced by an ordinary member and not taken up by the government is a private member's bill, and the defining feature is the absence of a government sponsor, which is what the stem describes when it says no minister will sponsor it. Such measures go through the same readings and divisions as any other, and they are not instruments made by a delegated authority, because they are proposed to the chamber rather than made under a power already granted. They are not consent measures either, because consent procedures apply to government business. The naming is settled by sponsorship, not by how narrow the subject matter is.
questions.hint: Ask who is putting the measure forward, since that is what fixes its category.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A money measure and financial priority
questions.learningObjective: identify the effect of restricted procedure on money measures
questions.stem: A chamber's rules allow a measure that only appropriates money or proposes a new charge to be introduced without notice and taken without amendment, leaving a short fixed period in which other members may object. What does such a rule do to the chamber's financial business?

options.text: It obliges the chamber to assent within the objection period or face the loss
options.misconception: turns a time limit on objection into a requirement to approve

options.text: It lets a money measure take effect before it has been read three times
options.misconception: claims an exemption from readings that the rule does not create

options.text: It removes the chamber's power to amend a money measure in any circumstances
options.misconception: denies the objection route that the rule expressly preserves

options.text: It gives money measures priority, so a measure cannot be stopped by a long debate

questions.explanation: The rule is a device for keeping public money moving. Money measures are the ones on which the rest of government waits, so a chamber gives them priority: a measure cannot be delayed by an ordinary debate, and the government's estimates do not drift into the next financial year because members wish to talk. What the rule does not do is remove the chamber's power altogether. The objection period is a real chance to object, and losing that argument is a defeat for the objection rather than an abolition of it. Nor does the rule touch the readings, which run as usual, and it imposes no duty on the chamber to assent: only the government's measure is at risk if the objection succeeds.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule is designed to prevent from delaying the public money.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A committee of supply
questions.learningObjective: explain the justification for examining estimates in committee
questions.stem: Instead of debating the government's estimates for each department in the chamber, a committee takes the estimates on evidence and the chamber later votes on the totals. What is the arrangement meant to achieve?

options.text: It spends members' time on scrutiny instead of on a long repetitive debate
It removes the spending decisions from the chamber's hands entirely
options.misconception: treats a change of forum as the removal of the chamber's decision

options.text: It allows individual members to move amendments to any single line
options.misconception: claims a line-by-line power that is the thing being replaced

options.text: It lets the government fix the totals without the chamber voting on them
options.misconception: denies the chamber a vote the arrangement is built around

questions.explanation: The point of taking estimates in committee is that the detail is where the argument is, and a full chamber is a poor place to conduct it. Scores of members are not on the committee, so the evidence on a department is taken in a setting where the few who care can question the few who answer, and the chamber then deals with the totals rather than repeating every line. That is a division of labour, not a removal: the chamber still votes, and the figures it votes on are the outcome of the scrutiny. Line-by-line amendment in the chamber is precisely what the arrangement is designed to replace, so the last option describes the opposite of the reform.
questions.hint: Ask what a full chamber is a poor setting for.

questions.topic: A ways and means committee
questions.learningObjective: explain why tax proposals are examined before the principle is debated
questions.stem: A committee with the exclusive task of examining proposals to raise money reports on a tax measure before the chamber debates it as a whole. Why place the examination at that point in the measure's progress?

options.text: So that the government's rate proposals become law without a division
options.misconception: claims the effect that removing a stage would have, not this one

options.text: So that any proposal failing to raise money cannot be examined at all
options.misconception: overstates the committee's remit into a bar on examining anything

options.text: So that a tax measure is never debated by the chamber as a whole
options.misconception: denies a chamber debate the arrangement is designed to feed

options.text: So that the principle of the charge is settled before the rates are argued

questions.explanation: Taxing is a measure with two separable parts: whether a charge ought to be imposed at all, and on what basis and at what rates. Putting the specialist examination first means the chamber argues the principle on the strength of what the rates would actually raise and whom they would fall on, instead of debating a principle in the dark and discovering the arithmetic afterwards. That is an ordering choice, not a way of excluding the chamber. A tax measure is still debated and still decided by the chamber, and the committee's work is to inform that debate rather than to remove it. Nothing in the arrangement either bars examination of anything or lets a rate schedule pass unvoted.
questions.hint: Ask which half of a tax measure needs the arithmetic worked out first.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A contingency reserve
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose and limits of a reserve line
questions.stem: A budget carries a single line for unforeseen needs from which the finance minister may spend without returning to the chamber, on condition that a statement of the draw is laid before it. What is that line for?

options.text: It lets the government spend freely, since no ceiling applies to the line
options.misconception: denies the ceiling that a line in an estimate necessarily carries

options.text: It requires the chamber to approve each draw before the money is spent
options.misconception: inverts the order of the statement and the spending

options.text: It replaces the appropriation, making the chamber's vote advisory only
options.misconception: turns a supplementary line into a substitute for the main vote

options.text: It absorbs shocks, so the chamber is not asked to vote again mid-year

questions.explanation: A reserve is an admission that a year will not go exactly to plan, and it is priced into the budget so the gap does not have to be handled by a fresh vote. Emergencies, overruns and sudden demands are met from a line that was approved once, with the chamber informed afterwards by statement, so an unforeseen event does not become a dispute about the budget as well. The line is still money in an estimate and carries a ceiling, so the freedom to spend is bounded. It supplements the appropriation rather than replacing it, and the condition runs in the opposite direction to the last option: the spending comes first and the account follows.
questions.hint: Ask what would otherwise have to happen when something unforeseen arose.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Commencement and entry into force
questions.learningObjective: read a commencement clause and state what follows from it

stimulus.body: Extract from an Act, written for this question. Section 1: This Act may be cited as the Inspection Reform Act. Section 2: (1) Sections 3 and 4 come into force on the day on which this Act is passed. (2) Sections 5 and 6 come into force on a day to be appointed by the Secretary of State, and different days may be appointed for different sections. (3) No appointment under subsection (2) may be made so as to come into force before the day on which this Act is passed. Section 3: An inspector appointed under section 5 shall hold the qualifications set out in Schedule 1. Section 4: In this Act 'qualifications' means the qualifications listed in Schedule 1 and no others. Section 5: The Secretary of State may appoint inspectors. Section 6: An inspector appointed before this Act is passed continues in office until replaced or released.

questions.stem: An Act provides that two of its sections come into force on the day it is passed, that two others come into force on a day the Secretary of State appoints, and that no appointment may be made so as to bring those sections into force before the day of passing. What follows from those words?

options.text: The two appointed sections can never be brought into force before the Act itself
The Act takes effect in full only once an appointing day has been fixed
options.misconception: ignores the two sections that take effect immediately on passing

options.text: The two immediate sections may be repealed before the appointed ones begin
options.misconception: finds a repeal power in a clause that says nothing about repeal

options.text: The Secretary of State may appoint a day earlier than passing for urgent work
options.misconception: contradicts the express limit in subsection (3) of the extract

questions.explanation: Subsection (3) is the operative limit: no appointment may be made so as to bring the appointed sections into force before the day the Act was passed, so those sections can never begin earlier than the Act itself. Read the rest with that, and the second option fails because sections 3 and 4 begin on the day of passing and the Act is not inert until an appointing day exists. The third option finds nothing in the extract to support it, since no provision about repeal appears. The fourth is excluded by the express words of subsection (3), which is exactly why that subsection is in the Act: to stop a section being made to operate at a time when the Act is not yet law.
questions.hint: Find the subsection that constrains the appointing day, then read it literally.

questions.learningObjective: read a delegation clause and state the extent of the power

(2) A person required under this standing order who fails to comply without adequate cause is guilty of an offence. (3) The committee may require the attendance of a Minister, and a Minister so attending may be questioned by the committee. (4) Nothing in this standing order authorises the committee to require a person to disclose a document the disclosure of which is prohibited by law. (5) This standing order applies to the committee and to any sub-committee appointed by it.

The member who is answerable for a department is the one who knows what has been done and what can be done, so the design is to have that person in the chamber when the chamber is looking at that department's business, and to allow an exception only on cause shown. The second option turns a duty owed by one minister into a bar on the chamber's decisions whenever any minister happens to be elsewhere, which the rule nowhere says. The third asks for more than attendance, since being present to answer is not the same as remaining through every debate. The fourth supplies a sanction from nothing: the rule attaches a duty and an exception, and no consequence for breach is described.
questions.hint: Ask who the rule is designed to have in the room, and about what.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A follow-up body without investigative power
questions.learningObjective: explain why a chamber would appoint a follow-up committee
questions.stem: A select committee examines one matter and reports, and the chamber then appoints a further committee to review whether the recommendations have been implemented, with no power to investigate again. Why would a chamber arrange it that way?

options.text: To comply with a rule that a select committee may report only once in a term
options.misconception: invents a rule the arrangement does not require to explain it

options.text: To make sure the first committee's report cannot be questioned or improved upon
options.misconception: describes a protection the chamber has no reason to want

options.text: To give the second committee wider powers than the first one had
options.misconception: reverses the arrangement, which removes a power rather than adding one

options.text: To keep the recommendations under review while avoiding the cost of a full inquiry

questions.explanation: An inquiry is expensive in sitting time, in officials' time and in political capital, and once one has been held there is usually little left to discover. A follow-up body with a narrower brief is a way of keeping a commitment visible without paying for a second investigation: it can check whether what was promised has been done and report that, and it cannot reopen the evidence. The arrangement is a division of labour between discovering and checking. The second option describes a protection nobody wants, since a chamber that could not question a report would have no reason to hold an inquiry at all. The third reverses the design, since the follow-up is expressly denied the power to investigate. And the fourth explains an arrangement that needs no explanation, because a follow-up body is a sensible step rather than a compliance requirement.
questions.hint: Ask what work still needs doing once an investigation has reported.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The money rule applied to a bill
questions.learningObjective: apply the money-measure rule to a bill that charges without appropriating
questions.stem: A bill is introduced that makes provision for charges on the public but contains no appropriation, and the chamber's rules treat any measure providing for such charges as a money measure. What follows?

options.text: The bill becomes a hybrid, so the chamber may amend it freely at any stage
options.misconception: invents a hybrid route that lets a restricted measure be freely amended

options.text: The bill escapes the rule, because it appropriates nothing already voted for
options.misconception: reads the absence of an appropriation as an exemption the rule does not grant

options.text: The bill is a money measure, so the restricted procedure applies to it
The bill must be withdrawn, since no measure may carry a charge of that kind
options.misconception: asserts a prohibition on charges that money measures exist to permit

questions.explanation: The trigger in the rules is provision for charges on the public, and the bill provides for charges, so it is caught. Whether it also happens to appropriate money is beside the point, because the purpose of the rule is to protect the timetable of anything that draws on public funds, and a measure that creates a charge draws on them. That makes the second option's reasoning wrong: an appropriation is not a condition of the classification. The third invents a route by which a restricted measure escapes restriction, and a hybrid arrangement in most systems still limits where amendment may be made. The fourth mistakes what the rule is for. Money measures are precisely the measures that may carry charges, and the restricted procedure is what makes them possible.
questions.hint: Find the condition in the rule that classifies a measure, and check only that.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Committee rules and control by small groups
questions.learningObjective: assess a reply to a criticism of a committee rule
questions.stem: A chamber changes its rules so that any member may call for a hearing of a witness of their own choosing, the committee must then proceed unless the majority objects, and the committee still reports in the usual way. A critic says this hands control to small groups. What is the strongest reply?

options.text: Small groups could already call witnesses informally, so nothing has actually changed
options.misconception: denies a rule that changes the formal default from refusal to compliance

options.text: The majority may object to every witness, so the rule takes nothing away from anyone
options.misconception: overstates the effect of the objection, which the rule does present as possible

options.text: The committee still has to produce the same report, so the change spends time rather than outcomes
Since a report may be made by a majority, the rule cannot affect the outcome of the inquiry
options.misconception: assumes a voting rule on a report the stem does not describe

questions.explanation: The strength of the reply is that it puts the cost in the right place. The rule changes who may put an item on the committee's agenda and makes compliance the default, and the price is committee time, which is a cost the chamber can control and can later reduce by changing the rule again. What it does not do is change the deliverable: the committee still reports in the same way, so a majority that dislikes what it hears has exactly the instrument it had before. The second option is too generous to the rule, since the stem makes objection possible rather than automatic, and an objection that is routinely overridden does not restore the status quo. The third denies that a written default matters. The fourth assumes the report is decided by a vote the stem does not describe.
questions.hint: Ask what the committee still has to produce at the end under the new rule.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the case for a second chamber rests on
questions.learningObjective: identify what a sceptical reply to a design argument concedes
questions.stem: Supporters of a second chamber argue that a single chamber can be carried by a transient majority and that a second chamber chosen on a different basis catches errors in the first. A sceptic replies that a second chamber can also be carried by a transient majority. What does that reply show?

options.text: That a second chamber always disagrees with the first more often than it agrees
options.misconception: asserts a pattern the sceptic's own reply does not establish

options.text: That the majority of the first chamber would otherwise have been permanent
options.misconception: assumes a permanence the supporters' case denies

options.text: That the argument turns on what a chamber does, not on how many chambers there are
That a second chamber is useless whenever its members are chosen on a separate list
options.misconception: turns one ground of criticism into a general verdict on a design

questions.explanation: The sceptic's reply attacks the count and not the function, and that is what makes it informative. If a second chamber can be swept the same way as a first, then the presence of a second chamber is not by itself the safeguard; what matters is the basis on which its members are chosen, the way it is selected and what it does with disagreement. So the reply concedes that the number of chambers is doing less work in the argument than the supporters assume, and pushes them onto the part of the case that is about function. The second option overreads that concession into declaring the design useless. The third asserts a permanence the supporters were denying. And the fourth claims a pattern of disagreement that the reply does not mention at all, since a chamber can be swept on a measure without being wrong about it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reply attacks how many chambers there are or what they do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Three features of a committee that can deliver
questions.learningObjective: select the conditions that let a committee produce a usable report
questions.stem: A select committee is to report within six months on a matter the chamber is expected to act on. Which three of the following most help it to reach a conclusion the chamber will act on?

options.text: A majority of members drawn from the parties that asked for the inquiry
options.misconception: mistakes who requested an inquiry for a guarantee of its standing

options.text: A fixed end date, so the inquiry cannot drift without producing anything
A power to require the department to give its evidence orally at the hearing
A membership drawn from more than one party, so no bloc can simply ignore the findings

questions.explanation: Three of the four conditions bear on whether the report will be acted on. Cross-party membership matters because a finding only survives if members of a bloc that dislikes it are prepared to sign the report rather than disown it. A fixed end date matters because an inquiry without one tends to finish when attention runs out, and a report that arrives too late is a report nobody acts on. A power to require evidence orally matters because the exchange is where a department's account is tested, and an inquiry that can only be satisfied by documents is an inquiry that can be satisfied by drafting. The third option confuses two different things. Who asked for the inquiry says something about why it exists, and a request by a majority does not by itself make the findings acceptable to anyone else, which is the opposite of what a report that is to be acted on requires.
questions.hint: Ask, of each condition, whether it changes what the report will contain or who will accept it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Conditions that make a finding bite
questions.learningObjective: select the mechanisms that convert a finding into action
questions.stem: A select committee finds that a department has been slow to publish the decisions it takes. Which three of the following would most help the chamber turn that finding into action?

options.text: Publication of the finding and the department's reply side by side
A larger membership, so that the finding carries more signatures beneath it
options.misconception: treats the number of signatures as a mechanism that moves a department

options.text: A rule barring a minister from answering any question until the reply is given
options.misconception: converts a duty to reply into a total bar on the minister's floor time

options.text: A rule requiring the department to reply in writing within a fixed period

questions.explanation: Two of the four change the position, and both work on the reply rather than on the finding. A fixed period for a written reply creates an occasion on which the department has to say what it will do, which is the point at which a commitment is easiest to extract, and publishing the finding and that reply together keeps them in view as a pair. The third option is a serious over-reach. Making the department answer is a reasonable demand; stopping a minister from answering any question at all is a different and disproportionate measure that would damage the chamber for a defect in one department. The fourth mistakes the size of a committee's membership for its authority. A finding signed by more members is still a finding, and what moves a department is a deadline and a visible commitment rather than a longer list of signatories.
questions.hint: Ask which of these changes what the department has to do, rather than what the report says.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Order of a scrutiny sequence
questions.learningObjective: sequence a scrutiny exercise on a delegated measure
questions.stem: A chamber's select committee is examining an instrument that was made under a delegated power. Put these four steps in the order in which they would normally fall.

options.text: The committee asks the department for its written explanation and the documents used
options.misconception: seeking the account after it has already tested the practice

options.text: The committee reports its findings to the chamber
options.misconception: reporting before the inquiry it reports on is finished

options.text: The committee takes evidence on how the instrument has worked in practice
options.misconception: taking evidence before the texts are read

options.text: The committee reads the enabling statute and the instrument made under it
options.misconception: leaving the texts to be read after the evidence has been taken

questions.explanation: The sequence runs from the documents to the account to the evidence to the conclusion. The committee must first read what it is examining, because the enabling statute fixes the limits of the power and the instrument is what the department did with it, and neither can be assessed before it has been seen. The written explanation and the documents behind it come next, so the department's account of its own reasoning is on the table before anybody is examined about it, which is the order that makes the evidence stage a test of that account rather than a hearing of it for the first time. Evidence on practice follows, and the report comes last because there is nothing to report until the inquiry is over.
questions.hint: Begin with the texts, and end with the step that depends on all of the others.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A duty tied to a result
questions.learningObjective: explain why an explanation is required as well as a target
questions.stem: A statute requires an authority, within a set time, to publish a report explaining why it has not met a target it was set. Why require the explanation as well as the target?

options.text: It obliges the authority to meet the target, since the duty is tied to it
options.misconception: assumes a reporting duty can compel the underlying result

options.text: It removes the need to set a target, since the duty is to explain rather than achieve
options.misconception: concludes that no target need be set at all

options.text: A published explanation makes the shortfall visible and open to challenge
It lets the authority revise the target once it has explained the shortfall
options.misconception: invents a power to change the target that the statute does not grant

questions.explanation: The explanation is what makes the target an accountability device rather than an aspiration. A target alone tells the reader what the authority was asked to achieve and nothing about what happened; a published explanation names the reason, in the authority's own words, at a time fixed in advance, and that is what allows the chamber, the press and the public to judge whether the reason is a difficulty or an excuse. Making the reason visible is the whole mechanism, and it is why the statute requires publication rather than merely an internal account. The second option asserts a result a reporting duty cannot produce. The third removes the target the duty is attached to, and the fourth invents a power to reset the target, which is a different provision from any the stem describes.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can do with a published explanation that a bare target does not allow.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The cost of a larger chamber
questions.learningObjective: explain the effect of chamber size on members' workload
questions.stem: Explain why enlarging a chamber raises the number of constituents each member has to represent, and say what follows for the time available for committee work.

answer.exemplar: Two mechanisms produce the effect, and they are different in kind. The first is divisibility. A member's obligations on behalf of constituents do not scale down when the constituency grows: a case that has to be taken up, a complaint that has to be pursued, a meeting that has to be attended. Divide a roughly fixed amount of such work among twice as many constituents and each member has half as much time for each of them, so the response to a single case is slower and the member is more stretched. The second is the shape of the chamber itself. A larger chamber needs more standing committees to cover the same portfolio and to hold the executive to account, and those committees need members. Members are the only resource a committee has, so the extra committees are staffed by taking members away from the other work. A further effect is procedural: more members means more opinions to reconcile, and committees that must produce a report acceptable across a wider range of views take longer to settle one. The result is that enlargement does not simply spread the same workload thinner. It adds committees at the same time as it multiplies casework, and both draw on the same limited supply of member time. A model answer should identify both mechanisms, should note that the two reinforce each other, and should avoid claiming that a larger chamber is simply less effective without saying through which channel it is.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies two distinct mechanisms rather than one. Divisibility handles the constituency side, because casework and representation demands do not shrink in proportion to the number of constituents a member has. The staffing of committees handles the chamber side, because a larger chamber needs more committees and members are the only thing a committee is made of. An answer that gives only the first leaves out the internal effect, and one that gives only the second leaves out why a member is less available. Crediting the interaction between the two is what makes the answer stronger still.
questions.hint: Ask what a member's fixed obligations divide between as the number of constituents grows.
